In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[complex analysis]], the '''Looman–Menchoff theorem''' states that a [[continuous function|continuous]] [[complex number|complex]]-valued function defined in an [[open set]] of the [[complex plane]] is [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] if and only if it satisfies the [[Cauchy–Riemann equations]].  It is thus a generalization of a [[Cauchy–Riemann equations#Goursat's theorem and its generalizations|theorem]] by [[Édouard Goursat]], which instead of assuming the continuity of ''f'', assumes its [[Fréchet derivative|Fréchet differentiability]] when regarded as a function from a subset of '''R'''<sup>2</sup> to '''R'''<sup>2</sup>. This theorem bears the name of Dutch mathematician [[Herman Looman (mathematician)|Herman Looman]] and Soviet mathematician [[Dmitrii Menshov]].

== Statement ==
A complete statement of the theorem is as follows:

* Let Ω be an open set in '''C''' and ''f'' : Ω → '''C''' be a continuous function.  Suppose that the [[partial derivative]]s <math>\partial f/\partial x</math> and <math>\partial f/\partial y</math> exist everywhere but a countable set in&nbsp;Ω.  Then ''f'' is holomorphic if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equation:
::<math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial\bar{z}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + i\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)=0.</math>

==Examples==

Looman pointed out that the function given by ''f''(''z'') = exp(−''z''<sup>−4</sup>) for ''z''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0, ''f''(0)&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations everywhere but is not analytic (or even continuous) at&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0. This shows that the function ''f'' must be assumed continuous in the theorem.

The function given by ''f''(''z'') = ''z''<sup>5</sup>/|''z''|<sup>4</sup> for ''z''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0, ''f''(0)&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 is continuous everywhere and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations at ''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, but is not analytic at ''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 (or anywhere else). This shows that a naive generalization of the Looman–Menchoff theorem to a single point is '''false''':

* Let ''f'' be continuous at a neighborhood of a point ''z'', and such that <math>\partial f/\partial x</math> and <math>\partial f/\partial y</math> exist at ''z''.  Then ''f'' is holomorphic at ''z'' if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equation at ''z''.
